title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
summary:
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy.
But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter.
Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels.

title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
summary:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

title: COP31 went up in flames over fossil fuels — it sends an important message
summary:
Anyone hoping for bold action on climate change has many reasons to be disappointed by the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31, which concluded in a dramatic overtime session on 22 November.
After gathering for nearly two weeks in the beach resort city of Antalya, Turkey, in what will probably be the hottest year on record, representatives from nearly all the world’s countries failed to agree on a plan to tackle climate change.
Almost 100 nations walked out without signing a ‘cover decision’ — a non-binding statement meant to push for ambitious action — because the document did not call on the world to transition away from fossil fuels.
The last COP climate talk to break down this badly was the Copenhagen summit in 2009.
But when language targeting fossil fuels disappeared from the draft cover decision after lobbying by oil-rich nations, a coalition of around 90 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, rejected the agreement.

title: ‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
summary:
A new report by UK-based charity Oxfam shows how Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’.
A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.
The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.
Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water.
Legal, political and financial risksOxfam says the destruction of Gaza’s water, food and sanitation systems may be relevant to alleged crimes under the Rome Statute and to assessing whether Israel violated the Genocide Convention.

title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
summary:

title: Urgent action needed to protect Buttermere, new reports warns
summary:
Tourism, infrastructure challenges and "outdated, undersized and poorly maintained" wastewater systems are contributing to the ecological decline of a popular lake, an environmental group has warned.
Buttermere, in the Lake District, has seen rising nutrient levels in recent years which can lead to excess phosphorus and blankets of algae.
West Cumbria Rivers Trust (WCRT), a charity which tracked down the sources of phosphorus for the study, argues "urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed".
The Buttermere Nutrient Investigations Project was commissioned and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) after the lake was last year found to be failing to meet total phosphorus targets.
WCRT said the investigation showed Buttermere - a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation - was a "fragile ecosystem under pressure".

title: Meta's AI boom just blew up its 2030 net-zero climate pledge after carbon emissions jumped 45% — and now it's backing 10 new gas power plants
summary:
The development comes as major technology companies encounter growing difficulties reconciling their expanding computing infrastructure with previously announced environmental commitments.
Meanwhile, electricity consumption increased 35% to 24.8 terawatt-hours, although the company said renewable and low-carbon contracts covered its entire electricity requirements.
The company is considering purchasing certificates associated with lower methane emissions to address some pollution associated with its anticipated natural gas consumption.
However, its growing dependence on electricity has consequences extending beyond carbon emissions, particularly regarding water consumption across its operations.
Although direct consumption declined 4%, usage in water-stressed locations increased 24%, while electricity-related water consumption climbed 37%.
